Datamonger brings public research datasets into your R analysis. It downloads
the registered files, checks their contents, and returns R objects you can work
with directly. You can also inspect where the data came from, find citations,
and record which version you used.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", error = FALSE)
```

## Fetch your first dataset

Load the package and fetch the Iris dataset from the UCI Machine Learning
Repository:

```{r}
#| label: load-package

library(datamonger)
```

```{r}
#| label: fetch-iris
#| eval: false

flowers <- fetch_data("uci:iris")
head(flowers)
```

The reference `"uci:iris"` combines the source (`uci`) and dataset name
(`iris`). You can also write `fetch_data("iris", source = "uci")`.

The first call downloads the data and stores a local copy for later use.
Downloading requires an internet connection. Download examples in this vignette
are shown without running them during the build.

Iris is returned as a data frame with 150 rows, four measurements, and a species
label. Datamonger preserves the registered column names, including spaces. Use
`[[` to select a column by name:

```{r}
#| label: plot-iris
#| eval: false

plot(
  flowers[["petal length"]],
  flowers[["petal width"]],
  xlab = "Petal length (cm)",
  ylab = "Petal width (cm)",
  pch = 19
)
```

Datamonger checks both the downloaded files and the decoded values before
returning the data. These checks help you detect a changed upstream file or an
unexpected interpretation of its contents.

## Find and inspect datasets

`list_data()` lists the datasets in the current registry, Datamonger's catalog
of dataset versions and their metadata. The package includes a registry, so you
can browse it without downloading anything. Here are the available dataset
references:

```{r}
#| label: browse-datasets

available <- list_data(offline = TRUE)
vapply(available, function(dataset) dataset$dataset_id, character(1))
```

Use `data_info()` to inspect a dataset before fetching it. Adding `@1` selects
version 1 explicitly:

```{r}
#| label: inspect-iris

info <- data_info("uci:iris@1", offline = TRUE)
info
info$license
```

Check each dataset's license and provenance before using it. `info$provenance`
describes its source, and `info$preprocessing` records known preparation steps.
Missing preprocessing metadata means that the history is not recorded. Fetching
the data does not apply the listed transformations again.

The `offline = TRUE` argument forbids network access. It works here because the
metadata is bundled with the package. You can omit it during normal use.

## Cite the data

`cite_data()` retrieves citation text from the registry without downloading the
dataset:

```{r}
#| label: cite-iris

cat(cite_data("uci:iris@1", offline = TRUE))
```

When the source recommends particular references, Datamonger selects them by
default. Use `include_all = TRUE` to see every recorded reference, or
`format = "records"` to work with the citation fields in R. Any upstream
citation instructions are included in the text output.

## Make an analysis reproducible

An unversioned reference such as `"uci:iris"` selects the registry's default
version. Once you choose data for an analysis, use an explicit version and
request the retrieval metadata:

```{r}
#| label: record-provenance
#| eval: false

registry <- active_registry()
result <- fetch_data("uci:iris@1", registry = registry, return_info = TRUE)
flowers <- result$data
result$info

saveRDS(list(registry = registry, info = result$info), "iris-provenance.rds")
```

The result separates the data from its metadata. `result$info` records the
dataset version, registry release, and digests used to verify the data. The
registry selector identifies the exact catalog used for the retrieval. Keep
these records with your analysis so that you can select the same catalog in a
later session:

```{r}
#| label: reuse-registry
#| eval: false

provenance <- readRDS("iris-provenance.rds")
flowers <- fetch_data("uci:iris@1", registry = provenance$registry)
```

## Reuse downloaded data

Datamonger keeps downloaded files in a cache. Later fetches check and reuse
those files. After downloading Iris, you can fetch it without network access:

```{r}
#| label: fetch-offline
#| eval: false

flowers <- fetch_data("uci:iris@1", offline = TRUE)
```

If a required file is missing from the cache, an offline fetch raises an error.
Download the datasets you need before disconnecting from the network.

Use `datamonger_cache_dir()` to find the default cache and `cache_info()` to
inspect its contents. To keep a separate cache for a project, pass the same
`cache_dir` to each call:

```{r}
#| label: project-cache
#| eval: false

flowers <- fetch_data("uci:iris@1", cache_dir = "data-cache")
cache_info(cache_dir = "data-cache")
```

`cache_clean()` removes cached downloads when you no longer need them. For
example, `cache_clean(dataset = "uci:iris@1", cache_dir = "data-cache")` removes
cached files associated with Iris from that cache. A later fetch can download
them again.

## Work with sparse data and splits

The return type follows the dataset's structure. CSV and TSV datasets become
data frames. LIBSVM and SVMLight datasets return a list with a sparse feature
matrix and a response vector:

```{r}
#| label: fetch-sparse
#| eval: false

heart <- fetch_data("libsvm:heart_scale@1")
dim(heart$features)
head(heart$response)
```

The feature matrix normally uses the `Matrix` package. Very large dimensions use
Datamonger's own sparse matrix class. Exact 64-bit integers use the
`datamonger_int64` class, which stores decimal strings to avoid losing
precision.

Datasets with predefined splits keep those splits separate. Access a split by
its name, such as `data[["train"]]` or `data[["test"]]`. Datamonger preserves
the provider's row membership; you decide how to prepare the data for your
analysis.

For more detail, see the help pages for `fetch_data()`, `data_info()`,
`cite_data()`, and `registry_selector()`.
